rows.verified: HSE guidance addresses occupational exposure to manufactured nanomaterials in the workplace.
The guidance supports compliance with COSHH when manufactured nanomaterials are used at work.
Employers using nanomaterials must protect employees from hazardous exposure.
Medium and large organisations may need specialist professional advice where control decisions are complex.
The guidance covers manufacture and manipulation of manufactured nanomaterials.
It specifically includes carbon nanotubes and other bio-persistent high-aspect-ratio nanomaterials.
The guidance was prepared in response to emerging evidence about nanomaterial toxicity.
General control principles can be applied to all workplace nanomaterials, with additional distinctions for CNTs and other bio-persistent HARNs.
Nanomaterial risk depends on particle composition, dimensions, persistence, surface chemistry, physical form, release potential, task and control effectiveness.
Nanomaterial evidence is material-, form-, process-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level toxicity probability.
The woodworking-machinery ACOP applies to most woodworking machinery other than hand-held tools and covers wood, corkboard, fibreboard and composite materials.
The ACOP provides practical guidance on safe use, information, training and guarding.
Where woodworking equipment presents specific risk, use should be restricted to trained and appointed people.
Operator instruction should cover machine hazards, limitations, kickback, guards, jigs, push-sticks, brakes, extraction and correct tooling.
After competence is demonstrated, written authorisation for particular machines and operations is good practice.
Vertical spindle moulders can cause contact injuries and can eject a tool part or workpiece if used incorrectly.
Woodworking risk assessment should examine workshop condition, guarding, braking, tooling, work at height and workplace transport.
PUWER control hierarchy prioritises fixed or interlocked guarding; where a circular-saw blade cannot be fully enclosed it must be protected as far as possible and supported by a safe system of work.
Woodworking-machinery risk depends on machine type, tooling, material, feed method, guarding, braking, extraction, training and intervention behaviour.
Woodworking evidence is machine-, material-, task-, tooling- and operator-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
